arms.predicted: The DFS timestamps approach will achieve a judge score of 100, matching the iter-1 BFS-based solution, because it produces mathematically identical routing decisions (subtree membership ≡ distance reduction on trees) while eliminating the O(n²) BFS bottleneck and ~2MB D[][] matrix. The freed cache and CPU budget provides more timing headroom.
arms.observed: Score: 100/100 on all 3 runs (100, 100, 100). The DFS timestamps + array adjacency solution achieves perfect scores with complete consistency across all runs. This includes the smoke test during preparation (also 100). The solution uses O(n) DFS precomputation instead of O(n²) BFS, eliminates the D[MAXN][MAXN] distance matrix entirely, and replaces distance comparisons with O(1) subtree membership checks via tin[]/tout[] arrays.
arms.diagnostic_note: Perfect 3/3 consistency at score 100 exceeds the iter-1 BFS-based solution's consistency (4/5 at 100, 1/5 at 95). The DFS approach provides strictly more timing headroom by eliminating the O(n²) precomputation phase, making the solution more robust to system load variance. Round counts are mathematically identical to the BFS version (verified by designer on all 20 test cases).

arms.predicted: The DFS timestamps approach with vector adjacency lists will score ≤99.4, because the vector overhead in per-round DP iteration (heap-allocated, non-contiguous memory access for child arrays) still causes enough slowdown to TLE on the largest test cases. This demonstrates that array-based adjacency is necessary regardless of the DFS improvement.
arms.observed: Score: 94.37 mean across 3 runs (94.37, 94.37, 99.37). The vector adjacency version scores consistently below 100, with 2/3 runs at 94.37 and 1/3 at 99.37. All scores are ≤99.4 as predicted. The magnitude of degradation (mean 96.03) is larger than the designer's exploration suggested (99.37), because the avx2 pragma had to be removed — #pragma GCC target("avx2") causes a compilation error with std::vector's allocator in GCC 13 (always_inline target mismatch). This makes the vector approach doubly penalized: it loses both contiguous-array cache efficiency AND the avx2 vectorization optimization.
arms.diagnostic_note: The ablation reveals two coupled costs of vector adjacency: (1) heap-allocated non-contiguous child arrays cause cache misses in the per-round DP inner loop (~2000 rounds × ~500 nodes), and (2) vector types are incompatible with the #pragma GCC target("avx2") optimization that the array version benefits from. The 5.63-point average gap (100 vs 96.03) is larger than the designer's predicted 0.63-point gap because both effects compound. This refines RP-3: array-based data structures are critical not just for cache efficiency but also for enabling compiler-level vectorization optimizations.

metadata.bundle_amendment: avx2 pragma removed due to compilation error with std::vector allocator

discrepancy_analysis: Both predictions confirmed. h-main scored 100 consistently (3/3 runs), confirming that DFS timestamps are a strict improvement over all-pairs BFS: identical routing decisions with O(n) instead of O(n²) precomputation. h-ablation scored ≤99.4 on all 3 runs (94.37, 94.37, 99.37), confirming that array-based adjacency remains necessary even with the DFS improvement. The ablation effect is larger than expected (mean 96.03 vs predicted ~99.37) because vector types additionally preclude avx2 optimization. The combined evidence establishes a clear optimization hierarchy: (1) algorithmic correctness (anti-oscillation + tree DP) provides the foundation (score 5→100), (2) array-based data structures enable cache efficiency and vectorization (score ~96→100), (3) DFS timestamps improve robustness by eliminating unnecessary O(n²) work.
